title: Finding peaks and troughs
objectives: Find stationary points and classify them.
Classify with the sign of $f'$ either side and with $f''$, and check the ends of a closed interval.

screens.prose: Drag P along the curve $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$. The line through P is the tangent, and the caption reads its slope.

derive.caption: At $x$ = {{fixed(P.x, 1)}} the slope of the tangent is {{fixed(3 * pow(P.x, 2) - 3, 2)}}

screens.question: Drag P from left to right over the hump. What happens to the slope as P passes the top?

options.text: It changes from positive to negative, passing through 0
It changes from negative to positive
options.why: That happens at the bottom of the dip, near $x = 1$. At the top of the hump the curve stops rising and starts falling.

options.text: It is at its largest at the top
options.why: You read the height of the curve. The top is the highest point, but there the tangent is flat: slope 0.

hints.text: Watch the sign of the slope just before and just after the top.
The top of the hump is near $x = -1$.
At $x = -1.5$ the slope is 3.75. At $x = -0.5$ it is −2.25. In between it passes 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption just before and just after P passes the top.

byKey.swap: You described the dip near $x = 1$. At the hump the curve goes from rising to falling.
byKey.height: You read the height, not the slope. At the top the tangent is flat.

explain.text: Just left of the top the slope is positive; just right of it the slope is negative. At $x = -1$ it is exactly 0, so the tangent is flat.

screens.prose: Same curve. The short lines are the tangents at five points A to E.
screens.question: Tap every point where the tangent is flat.

hints.text: A flat tangent is horizontal, parallel to the $x$-axis.
Look at the top of the hump and the bottom of the dip.

feedback.correct: B and D: the top of the hump and the bottom of the dip.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap only the points whose tangent is horizontal.

byKey.highest: You tapped the two highest points. E is as high as B, but the curve is still climbing there: slope 9.
byKey.crossing: You tapped where the curve crosses the axis. The height is 0 there, but the slope is −3.
byKey.A: At A the curve climbs steeply: slope 9.
byKey.C: At C the curve is falling: slope −3. A height of 0 is not a slope of 0.
byKey.E: At E the curve climbs steeply: slope 9. Being as high as B does not make it flat.
byKey.B: You missed B, the top of the hump. A peak has a flat tangent too.
byKey.D: You missed D, the bottom of the dip. A trough has a flat tangent too.

explain.text: You tapped B and D, where $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 0$, so $x = \pm 1$. B tops a hump and D bottoms a dip. At A, C and E the curve is still climbing or falling.

screens.prose: A point where $f'(x) = 0$ is called a **stationary point**: for an instant the curve neither rises nor falls. Here is a new curve, $g(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 1$.
screens.question: Find both stationary points of $g$.

hints.text: Differentiate $g$, then solve $g'(x) = 0$.
$g'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9$. Take out the common factor 3.
$3(x^2 - 4x + 3) = 3(x - 1)(x - 3)$, so $x = 1$ or $x = 3$. Put each back into $g$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $g'(x) = 0$, then put each $x$ back into $g$.

byKey.r0c2: You need $g(1)$, the height of the curve: $1 - 6 + 9 + 1$.
byKey.r1c2: You need $g(3)$, the height of the curve: $27 - 54 + 27 + 1$.

explain.text: $g'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9 = 3(x - 1)(x - 3)$, which is 0 at $x = 1$ and $x = 3$. Putting these into $g$ gives $g(1) = 5$ and $g(3) = 1$.

screens.prose: Is (1, 5) a peak or a trough? Check the slope just either side of it. The tangents show $g'(0.5)$ and $g'(1.5)$.
screens.question: What kind of stationary point is (1, 5)?

options.why: You matched + then − to a dip. Rising and then falling makes a peak.

options.text: Neither, because $g'$ is not 0 at 0.5 or 1.5
options.why: You expected the test points to be flat. They sit either side of the stationary point, so only their signs matter.

hints.text: A positive slope means rising; a negative slope means falling.
Read the two slope labels: 3.75 on the left and −2.25 on the right.
The curve rises into $x = 1$ and falls out of it. That shape is a peak.

feedback.correct: Rising into it, falling out of it: a peak.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the sign of the slope on each side of $x = 1$.

explain.text: The slope goes from 3.75 to −2.25: rising, flat, falling. So (1, 5) is a **local maximum**, higher than every point near it. At (3, 1) the signs run − then +, which makes it a **local minimum**.

screens.prose: Differentiate again: $g''(x) = 6x - 12$ is the slope of the slope. The dashed curve is $g'$, with its tangent drawn at $x = 3$.
screens.question: Use $g''(3)$ to classify the stationary point (3, 1).

options.text: $g''(3) = 6 > 0$, so it is a local minimum
$g''(3) = 6 > 0$, so it is a local maximum
options.why: You read positive as a peak. $g'' > 0$ means $g'$ is increasing: from negative, through 0, to positive. That is a dip.
You substituted into $g'$, which is 0 at every stationary point. Substitute 3 into $g''(x) = 6x - 12$.

hints.text: Substitute $x = 3$ into $g''(x) = 6x - 12$.
A positive $g''$ means $g'$ is increasing: it climbs through 0.
$g''(3) = 6$. So $g'$ goes from negative to positive at 3: falling, then rising.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $g''(3)$, then ask whether $g'$ climbs or falls through 0.

explain.text: $g''(3) = 18 - 12 = 6 > 0$, so $g'$ climbs through 0 there: $g$ falls, then rises. That makes (3, 1) a local minimum. At (1, 5), $g''(1) = -6 < 0$: a maximum, as you found.

screens.prose: Both $x^3$ and $x^4$ have a stationary point at 0. Their second derivatives, $6x$ and $12x^2$, are both 0 there too.
screens.question: What kind of point is $x = 0$ for each curve?

options.text: Neither, for both, because the second derivative is 0
options.why: You read $f''(0) = 0$ as a verdict. It is no verdict: $x^4$ has a clear dip at 0.
Left of 0, $x^3$ is negative, below its value at 0. So 0 is not its lowest point nearby.
You swapped them. $x^4 \ge 0$ everywhere, so 0 is its lowest point.

hints.text: When the second derivative is 0, go back to the sign of the first derivative either side.
$3x^2$ is positive on both sides of 0. $4x^3$ is negative on the left and positive on the right.
$x^3$ rises, flattens and keeps rising: neither. $x^4$ falls, then rises: a minimum.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the sign of each first derivative on both sides of 0.

explain.text: $f''(0) = 0$ gives no verdict, so we used the signs of $f'$. $x^3$ rises on both sides: a **stationary point of inflection**, neither peak nor trough. $x^4$ falls, then rises: a minimum.

screens.prose: Back to $g(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 1$, now only on the closed interval $0 \le x \le 5$. You found a local maximum at (1, 5).
screens.question: What is the largest value of $g$ on $0 \le x \le 5$?

widget.label: Largest value of g on the interval

hints.text: Where can the largest value on a closed interval sit?
Compare $g$ at the stationary points with $g$ at both ends.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $g$ at the stationary points and at both ends.

byKey.local-max: You took the local maximum at $x = 1$. It only beats its neighbours; the curve climbs past it to 21 at $x = 5$.
byKey.smallest: 1 is the smallest value, at $x = 0$ and $x = 3$. The question asks for the largest.

explain.text: The largest value sits at the end: $g(5) = 125 - 150 + 45 + 1 = 21$. A local maximum only beats the points near it. On a closed interval, always check the ends too.

screens.prose: You classified stationary points in two ways. Where $f'(a) = 0$: $$f''(a) < 0 \Rightarrow \text{local max}, \qquad f''(a) > 0 \Rightarrow \text{local min}.$$ If $f''(a) = 0$, use the sign of $f'$ either side. On a closed interval, check the ends as well.
screens.question: At $x = a$, $f'(a) = 0$ and $f'$ changes from negative to positive. What is $a$?

options.why: You swapped the patterns. Falling and then rising makes a dip.
At a stationary point of inflection $f'$ keeps its sign, as for $x^3$. Here the sign changes.

hints.text: A negative slope means the curve is falling.
Falling into $a$ and rising out of it: the curve dips at $a$.

feedback.correct: Falling, then rising: a local minimum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn each sign into falling or rising, then picture the shape.

explain.text: Negative then positive means the curve falls into $a$ and rises out of it. That is the trough pattern you saw at (3, 1).

screens.prose: Why does $f''(a) > 0$ give a minimum? The sign test already explains it. Each line gives its reason.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: $f''$ is the slope of $f'$, so $f'$ is increasing near $a$
An increasing $f'$ that is 0 at $a$ is negative just left of $a$ and positive just right
So $f$ falls and then rises: $a$ is a local minimum

hints.text: Start from what is given.
The middle lines turn a fact about $f''$ into the signs of $f'$.
Given, then $f'$ increasing, then the signs of $f'$, then the shape of $f$.

feedback.correct: Each line follows from the one before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from what is given and end with the shape of $f$.

byKey.d3: You jumped to the signs of $f'$. First say why $f'$ is increasing.
byKey.d4: The shape of $f$ is the conclusion, so it comes last.
byKey.d2: Start from what is given before using it.

explain.text: $f'' > 0$ makes $f'$ increase, and an increasing $f'$ can only pass 0 from below. Negative then positive is the trough pattern. Swap every sign and the same argument gives $f''(a) < 0 \Rightarrow$ a maximum.

screens.prose: A portfolio puts weight $w$ in stock A and $1 - w$ in stock B. A has volatility 20%, B has 30%, and they are uncorrelated. The variance of the portfolio is $$V(w) = 0.04w^2 + 0.09(1 - w)^2.$$
screens.question: Which weight $w$ gives the smallest variance? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Differentiate $V$ and solve $V'(w) = 0$.
$V'(w) = 0.08w - 0.18(1 - w)$. The chain rule gives the minus sign on the second term.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $V'(w) = 0.26w - 0.18$ equal to 0.

byKey.inverse-vol: You weighted by inverse volatility, 5 to 3.33. Minimum variance weights by inverse variance, so A gets more: $\tfrac{0.09}{0.13}$.
byKey.all-a: You put everything in the calmer stock. At $w = 1$ the slope is still 0.08, so moving some weight into B lowers the variance.
byKey.equal: Equal weights give variance 0.0325. The slope there is $-0.05$, so the variance still falls as $w$ grows.

explain.text: $V'(w) = 0.26w - 0.18 = 0$ gives $w = \tfrac{9}{13} \approx 0.692$, and $V''(w) = 0.26 > 0$ confirms a minimum. The variance is 0.0277, a volatility of about 16.6%. That is below either stock on its own.

ideas: A stationary point is where $f'(x) = 0$: the tangent is flat.
Classify it by the sign of $f'$ either side, or by $f''$: negative means a peak, positive a trough.
When $f''(a) = 0$ the second test is silent. On a closed interval the largest value can sit at an end.

formula.name: Second derivative test
formula.note: If $f''(a) = 0$, use the sign of $f'$ either side, as for $x^3$ and $x^4$.

summary.trap: A local maximum only beats its neighbours. On a closed interval, compare it with the ends.

quiz.question: At which $x$ does $f$ have a local maximum?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $f'(x) = 0$, then use $f''$ to tell the peak from the trough.

byKey.min: You found the other stationary point. $f''(2) = 12 > 0$, so $x = 2$ is the trough.
byKey.zero: You solved $f(x) = 0$ or $f''(x) = 0$. Stationary points come from $f'(x) = 0$.

explain.text: $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12 = 0$ gives $x = \pm 2$. $f''(x) = 6x$ is $-12$ at $x = -2$, so that point is a local maximum, with $f(-2) = 16$.

quiz.question: What kind of stationary point is $x = 0$?

options.text: Neither: $f'$ is negative on both sides

options.why: Just right of 0, $f'$ is negative, so $f$ keeps falling past 0. It is not a lowest point.
Just left of 0, $f'$ is negative too, so $f$ falls into 0. It is not a highest point.
$f''(0) = 0$ only silences the second test. The sign of $f'$ either side still decides.

feedback.correct: A stationary point of inflection: $f$ falls, flattens, and falls on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the sign of $4x^2(x - 3)$ just left and just right of 0.

explain.text: Near 0, $4x^2 > 0$ and $x - 3 < 0$, so $f'(x) < 0$ on both sides. The curve falls, flattens at 0, and keeps falling. The minimum is at $x = 3$, where $f''(3) = 36 > 0$.

quiz.prose: $f(x) = x^2 - 4x$ on the closed interval $0 \le x \le 5$.
quiz.question: What is the largest value of $f$ on this interval?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the stationary value with both ends.

byKey.stationary: $f(2) = -4$ is the only stationary value, and it is the minimum. The maximum must be at an end.
byKey.left-end: That is the left end. The right end, $f(5) = 5$, is higher.

explain.text: $f'(x) = 2x - 4 = 0$ only at $x = 2$, where $f(2) = -4$ is the minimum. The ends give $f(0) = 0$ and $f(5) = 5$, so the largest value is 5.

quiz.question: What is the largest value of $f$? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the product rule, solve $f'(x) = 0$, then find $f$ there.

byKey.x-value: 1 is where the maximum is. The question asks for the value: $f(1) = e^{-1}$.
byKey.e: You computed $e^{1}$. The function is $x e^{-x}$, so at $x = 1$ it is $e^{-1}$.

explain.text: $f'(x) = e^{-x} - x e^{-x} = (1 - x)e^{-x}$, which is 0 only at $x = 1$. The sign goes + then −, so it is a maximum. $f(1) = e^{-1} \approx 0.368$; at $x = 0$ the value is 0.
